docs.title: Catch-up summary
docs.text:
The master's thesis is complete. Two things are in progress now:

  • A paper for the journal Computers, Environment and Urban Systems (CEUS), in drafting. It presents the method from the thesis: for each GPS stay, it gives a probability that the person was in a building, on a street, or in an open space, instead of picking one place. The model learns from 907 stays with known answers from a field survey in Hiroshima. On data it has not seen, it picks the correct type for 71.6% of stays (grouped CV accuracy 0.716 ± 0.076), and it does better there than Random Forest and XGBoost. Its main weakness, mistaking streets and open spaces for buildings, comes from how the street map is cut into many short pieces, not from the GPS data itself. Start from Thesis summary.
  • A poster and a presentation for CSIS DAYS 2026, in drafting.

docs.title: About this research
docs.text:
Hafiyyan Hilmy Fawwaz · Urban Transportation and Planning Lab, Hiroshima University

A GPS staypoint rarely tells you which place a person actually visited: positional error is often larger than the gap between a building, the street in front of it and the open space beside it. This research builds a probabilistic framework that assigns each staypoint to an urban spatial entity (building, street or open space) under explicit positional uncertainty, instead of snapping it to the nearest one.

Dates are written DD-MM-YYYY.

docs.title: Alpha calibration
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

How the setting α was chosen. α controls how fast the f_distance score falls as a candidate gets farther from the stay.

The method is called profile likelihood, and it uses Model 4a. Take one value of α, fit all the other weights again, and record how well the model fits (LL(b), closer to 0 is better). Repeat for many values of α and keep the best one. Because \(f_\text{distance}(\alpha) = f_\text{distance}(1)^{1/\alpha^2}\), the scores do not need to be computed again for each α.

α LL(b) Accuracy 1.0 -0.6881 0.717 2.0 -0.6708 0.726 2.4 -0.6701 0.723 3.0 -0.6707 0.720 4.0 -0.6725 0.720

The fit has one clear best point. The optimizer finds α* = 2.4297. Computing the scores again from scratch at this value gives the same result as the shortcut, to within 2e-16.

  • Model 2 has its own best α (2.106). Using that value in Model 4a costs almost nothing, and the reverse is also true. So the two models agree on how fast the score should fall.
  • Tune α once on Model 4a, then build the later models with that value. Tuning α again inside the larger Models 5 and 6 improved the fit only a little, lowered accuracy, and about doubled the VIF warning values.
  • Model 1 has no single best α, and no value of α fixes its main problem (Model 1: base).

The main result of this step: The f_distance² artifact. With the full, unthinned data, the best α moves: Raw-density alpha profile. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Candidate density bias toward building
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

Why the model often says "building" when the correct answer is street or open space.

A first guess would be that street stays have too few street candidates. The data shows the opposite. Stays that really were on a street have the most candidates of their own type:

True type Same-type candidates, mean median Total candidates, mean Building 7.09 5 22.99 Street 13.17 11 36.61 Open space 5.42 3 18.34

The share_type term gives a lower value to a candidate with many neighbours of the same type (the weight share_street is -8.09 in the Final model). The map stores streets as many short pieces next to each other (Spatial entity layers). So a stay on a street is punished for a crowd of street pieces that the map itself created. The probability then moves to the nearest building (Confusion matrix).

This comes from the street map, so it can be fixed. The GPS data itself does not set the limit (Contributions). But it weakens the argument that streets are real places of activity: Tension with the street-space argument, Candidate density as boundary-matching difficulty.

Part of Error analysis.

docs.title: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area
docs.text:
Analysis Master 29-07-2026

With the same search distance (R_buffer = 10 m), the full survey data produced 36,110 candidate rows, and the thinned data 22,484. That is 1.6 times more candidates for the same 907 stays.

This is expected. Candidate selection draws a circle around every GPS point of a stay. The full data has about 9.9 times more points, and more circles cover more ground, even with the same radius. So thinning the data also makes the search area smaller, not only the number of points. Keep this in mind if the search distance is tested again (R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m).

Part of Raw-density refit.

docs.title: Confusion matrix
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

A table of the Final model's answers against the correct answers. Each row is the correct type, each column is the model's answer. Every answer comes from a test where that stay was not used for learning (grouped cross-validation).

actual predicted building street open space recall building 476 22 33 89.6% street 86 79 20 42.7% open space 86 11 94 49.2%

Recall is the share of stays of one type that the model found. For example, 79 of 185 street stays were called street: 42.7%.

  • The model finds building stays about twice as often as the other two types.
  • When it gets a street or open-space stay wrong, it mostly says building (46.5% and 45.0% of those stays). It rarely mixes up street and open space (10.8% and 5.8%).
  • More street stays were called building (86) than street (79).

On the training data the table looks almost the same (building 89.8%, street 44.3%, open space 49.7%). So overfitting does not explain this pattern.

Why it happens: Candidate density bias toward building. How it changes from test set to test set: Fold difficulty. Answers RQ2 of Research questions. Part of Error analysis.

docs.title: Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Is f_directional useful only for streets? Two versions were compared. 3a is Model 2: share-type and sigma unchanged, with the direction score for every candidate. 3b sets the direction score to 0 for buildings and open spaces, so only streets keep it:

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{dir,street} + w_4\,share_\text{bldg} + w_5\,share_\text{street} + w_6\,share_\text{os} + w_7\,\sigma\]

Both versions have 7 parameters, so they can be compared directly.

R=10 m 3a: shared 3b: street only LL(b) -0.7510 -0.7520 Accuracy 0.668 0.666 Building / street / open space 0.872 / 0.362 / 0.398 0.872 / 0.335 / 0.414 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.664 ± 0.046 0.658 ± 0.040 Condition number 117 135
  • Keeping the score only for streets does not help. The fit is a little worse and the model is less stable (the direction score's VIF is 9.26 instead of 7.11).
  • It only moves accuracy from street to open space.
  • In 3b, share_bldg becomes significant (t goes from 0.76 to 2.54). So whether share_bldg matters depends on how the direction score is set up.

3a was kept. The same result came back later with the tuned α, in f_directional: shared vs split. Next: Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: f_directional: shared vs split
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Does f_directional need a separate weight for each place type ("split", the 14-parameter model, \(w_{3,t} f_\text{directional}\))? Or is one weight for all types enough ("shared", 12 parameters, \(w_3 f_\text{directional}\))? Everything else stayed the same.

Shared (12) Split (14) Street only (12) Accuracy 0.721 0.724 0.723 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.716 ± 0.076 0.709 ± 0.075 0.716 ± 0.069 Condition number 1,373 2,430 1,431

Split vs shared: LR = 5.41, df = 2, p = 0.067. This is not significant: the two extra weights do not improve the fit enough. They raise training accuracy by 0.3 percentage points, but lower accuracy on unseen data and double the condition number. That is overfitting (Overfitting signature).

The shared weight is clearly significant (t = +3.12). In the split version, only the building weight passes 1.96. "Street only" performs about the same as shared at this size, and never better. In the 7-parameter models, shared wins on every measure (CV 0.666 against 0.656), the same result as in Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b).

Decision: shared, 12 parameters → Final model, the final model of the thesis (Section 5.1.8). Part of Calibration.

Linked from Calibration · Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) · Overfitting signature · RQ1 rebuilt with grouped CV · Stepwise VIF elimination · f_directional

docs.title: The f_distance² artifact
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

With α = 1, a squared distance term (f_distance²) looked clearly significant (t = 3.81) in the Interaction term screen (α = 1). After Alpha calibration set α to 2.4297, the same test, run again from the start, gives only t = 0.50.

So the squared term was not finding a real curve in the data. It was making up for a distance score that fell too fast because α was too small. It also caused most of the instability of Model 6.

Screen term t at α = 1 t at α = 2.4297 f_distance² 3.81 0.50 σ² 2.23 2.47 f_distribution × σ -0.15 0.32 f_distance × f_directional 0.11 1.73 f_distribution × share_type 5.58 4.91

Lesson: after changing α, choose the extra terms again from the start. Keeping the old terms and only changing α doubled the VIF warning values (condition number from 20,695 to 48,275).

One case of Overfitting signature. Next: Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. Part of Calibration.

docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

How closely each pair of the Final model's 12 inputs move together. A correlation near 1 or -1 means two inputs carry almost the same information. Near 0 means they are unrelated.

(dist = f_distribution, dec = f_distance, dir = f_directional, shr = share; _b/_s/_o = building/street/open space.)

The strongest pairs are always inputs of the same type: f_distance and share for open space (.92), street (.91) and building (.87). Multicollinearity is structural explains why. f_directional has one shared weight, but it still moves with the street distance score and the street share (.71, .66). docs.title: Final model
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The model the thesis ends with (Section 5.1.8). It has 12 parameters, uses α = 2.4297 and a search distance (R_buffer) of 10 m.

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + w_6\,(f_\text{distribution}\times share_\text{type})\]

A small \(t\) means the weight is different for each place type (building, street, open space). No \(t\) means one weight shared by all types.

How well it fits. The most important line is CV accuracy: on data it did not learn from, the model picks the correct type for 71.6% of stays.

LL(0) / LL(C) / LL(b) -1.0799 / -0.9362 / -0.6557 ρ² vs LL(0) / LL(C) 0.393 / 0.300 Accuracy (in-sample) 0.721 CV accuracy (grouped, 5-fold) 0.716 ± 0.076 CV building / street / open space 0.896 / 0.429 / 0.491 Condition number 1,373

The weights. w is the learned weight: positive raises the probability, negative lowers it. t shows how clearly the weight differs from zero (about 2 or more is significant). VIF shows overlap with other inputs (above 10 is the usual warning line; see Multicollinearity is structural).

Term w t VIF f_distribution, bldg +1.253 2.19 5.62 f_distribution, street +0.913 1.57 5.37 f_distribution, os +5.277 8.10 3.61 f_distance, bldg -2.102 -2.04 9.37 f_distance, street -2.293 -2.51 21.42 f_distance, os -6.554 -6.14 13.05 f_directional +0.980 3.12 10.28 share, bldg -3.152 -4.64 7.90 share, street -8.088 -9.57 11.95 share, os -5.873 -4.17 10.13 sigma +0.778 5.89 3.14 f_distribution × share_type +5.779 5.66 9.81

docs.title: Fold difficulty
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

Cross-validation splits the data into 5 test sets (folds). This table shows the Final model's accuracy in each one:

Fold Total Building Street Open space 0 0.635 0.896 0.162 0.368 1 0.665 0.906 0.324 0.333 2 0.801 0.897 0.667 0.658 3 0.791 0.877 0.622 0.718 4 0.685 0.906 0.368 0.378

Building accuracy hardly changes (0.877-0.906). Street accuracy changes by more than 4 times (0.162-0.667). Each fold has about the same number of street stays (36-38), so the changes do not come from small numbers. Folds 0 and 1 are the hardest for every type, and also for Random Forest and XGBoost (ML ceiling check, row level). So the difficulty comes from which stays end up in a fold, not from one place type.

docs.title: Interaction term screen (α = 1)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Could combined or squared terms help the model? Five such terms were tested together, on top of the 7-parameter model with shared weights. An interaction term multiplies two inputs, for example f_distribution × σ. A term with a t-value above about 2 counts as significant.

Term w t f_distance² +4.588 3.81 significant σ² +0.165 2.22 significant f_distribution × σ -0.058 -0.15 f_distance × f_directional +0.150 0.11 f_distribution × share_type +5.264 5.57 significant, largest

The three significant terms were added to Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters. This gives Model 6, with 16 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + w_6\,f_\text{distance}^2 + w_7\,\sigma^2 + w_8\,(f_\text{distribution}\times share_\text{type})\] 4a Model 6 (α = 1) Accuracy 0.717 0.724 Building / street / open space 0.902 / 0.443 / 0.466 0.876 / 0.497 / 0.524 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.707 ± 0.069 0.711 ± 0.077 Condition number 775 20,695

Model 6 is the first model that improves open space (to 0.524), but building accuracy drops a little. Inside the larger model, σ² stops working (t falls to -0.27). And f_distance² turns out to make up for an α that was not yet tuned: The f_distance² artifact.

The two terms that were not significant are built from inputs that overlap strongly (VIF up to 73). So "not significant" is weak evidence for them.

The same test with the tuned α: Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: ML baseline, stay level (superseded)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 20-07-2026

Sensei asked whether Random Forest or XGBoost could show the best possible result, since these methods can find curved and combined effects by themselves. Both were trained to choose one of three types, using the same 13 inputs as the simple model, one row per stay, with no combined terms added by hand. They were tested with normal (not grouped) cross-validation.

Model CV accuracy Building Street Open space Logit (14 params) 0.716 ± 0.035 RF 0.754 ± 0.023 0.913 0.573 0.487 RF, class-weighted 0.753 ± 0.017 0.917 0.562 0.482 XGBoost 0.723 ± 0.015 0.855 0.557 0.518 XGBoost, class-weighted 0.725 ± 0.012 0.838 0.600 0.534

"Class-weighted" means the less common types (street, open space) were given more importance during training.

At the time, this looked like room for a small improvement (Random Forest +3.8 percentage points). Every tree model scored 1.000 on its own training data, which means it memorized the data.

Replaced: normal cross-validation lets recordings of the same stop from different phones end up in both training and testing (Grouped cross-validation). The fair comparison turns the ranking around: ML ceiling check, row level. The finding about σ still holds: Sigma in tree importance.

Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: ML ceiling check, row level
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

A fair comparison between the simple model and two machine-learning models. Random Forest and XGBoost got exactly the same task as the simple model (one row per stay and candidate), the raw inputs plus the place type, and exactly the same grouped test sets.

Model In-sample CV (grouped) CV building CV street CV open space Logit, Final model 0.721 0.716 ± 0.076 0.896 0.429 0.491 Random Forest 0.762 0.699 ± 0.063 0.942 0.439 0.277 XGBoost 0.849 0.695 ± 0.071 0.893 0.461 0.371

Both tree models win on the training data (in-sample), and both lose on unseen data (CV). Almost the whole difference comes from open space. For building and street, the three models are close. So with a fair test, the machine-learning models offer no improvement. This reverses the earlier result in ML baseline, stay level (superseded).

Settings: Random Forest with 400 trees, depth 8, at least 5 rows per leaf. XGBoost with 300 rounds, depth 4, learning rate 0.1. Neither was tuned. All three models find the same test sets hard (Fold difficulty).

The clearest case of Overfitting signature. Which inputs the trees use: Sigma in tree importance. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Model 1: base
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The first and simplest model: the four scores, each with one weight shared by all place types.

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{temporal} + w_4 f_\text{directional}\]

Tested with two search distances, 10 m and 15 m:

R=10 m R=15 m LL(C) / LL(b) -0.9362 / -0.9745 -0.9985 / -1.0360 ρ² vs LL(C) -0.041 -0.038 Accuracy 0.518 0.509 Building / street / open space 0.576 / 0.378 / 0.492 0.589 / 0.346 / 0.445 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.514 ± 0.089 0.512 ± 0.098 Condition number 36 26 Term (R=10 m) w t VIF f_distribution +3.331 5.34 7.14 f_distance -0.467 -1.14 3.73 f_temporal +0.179 0.29 7.49 f_directional -0.080 -0.41 2.78
  • Worse than a simple baseline. ρ² is negative, so this model does worse than just knowing how common each type is. No value of α fixes this (Alpha calibration).
  • Only f_distribution is significant at both distances. f_temporal moves almost the same way as f_distribution (r ≈ 0.88), so it was removed.
  • f_distance has a negative weight at 10 m (-0.47) and a positive one at 15 m (+0.95). This had to wait until α was tuned.
  • The condition number is low, so the fit itself is stable. The problem is which inputs the model has, not the fitting.

Next: Model 2: share-type and sigma. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Model 2: share-type and sigma
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The second model removes f_temporal. It adds share_type, with a separate weight for each type, and one sigma term:

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{directional} + w_4\,share_\text{bldg} + w_5\,share_\text{street} + w_6\,share_\text{os} + w_7\,\sigma\] R=10 m R=15 m ρ² vs LL(C) 0.198 0.199 Accuracy 0.668 0.654 Building / street / open space 0.872 / 0.362 / 0.398 0.881 / 0.308 / 0.356 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.664 ± 0.046 0.647 ± 0.042 Condition number 117 98 Term (R=10 m) w t f_distribution +3.542 8.40 f_distance -1.209 -2.60 f_directional +1.708 5.89 share_bldg +0.219 0.76 share_street -5.552 -15.68 share_os -5.887 -12.79 sigma +0.475 5.87
  • The model now beats the simple baseline, and accuracy is 15 percentage points higher than Model 1: base.
  • Almost all of the gain is for buildings. Building accuracy jumps from about 0.58 to about 0.87. Street stays the same or gets worse, and open space gets worse. The large negative weights share_street and share_os push the probability toward buildings. This is an early sign of Candidate density bias toward building.
  • sigma has a clear positive effect. f_directional becomes significant once f_temporal is removed.
  • The weight of f_distance now changes sign between 10 m and 15 m, and both values are significant.

docs.title: Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

In this model, every score gets its own weight for each place type (building, street, open space). This is called "alternative-specific". sigma keeps one shared weight. In total, 13 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma\] Model 4a (R=10 m, α=1) ρ² vs LL(C) 0.265 LR vs 3a (df=6) 114.15, p < 1e-16 Accuracy 0.717 Building / street / open space 0.902 / 0.443 / 0.466 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.707 ± 0.069 Condition number 775

The LR test compares this model with model 3a, which has shared weights. The result is very clear (p < 1e-16): separate weights per type fit much better.

For the first time, all three types improve together (building +3 percentage points, street +8.1, open space +6.8). The highest VIF is 10.69, for f_directional_street. The strong overlap between inputs of the same type is explained in Multicollinearity is structural.

f_distance_bldg and f_distance_street are not significant on their own (t = 0.29 and 0.34). Once weights are split by type, part of the distance information is picked up by share and sigma.

All later models build on this one. Next: Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected), Interaction term screen (α = 1). α was tuned on this model: Alpha calibration. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters plus two constants, asc_street and asc_os. A constant (ASC) is a fixed extra value for each type, which shows whether a type is preferred in general. Building is the reference (\(ASC_\text{bldg} = 0\)). In total, 15 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + ASC_t\] 4a 5 (+ ASC) Accuracy 0.717 0.728 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.707 ± 0.069 0.717 ± 0.068 LR vs 4a (df=2) 29.6, p < 0.0001 Max VIF 10.69 39.76 Condition number 775 37,583

On paper, the constants are significant. But the gain on unseen data is smaller than the normal spread between test sets. And asc_street and f_directional_street move almost together (r = 0.96). The reason: f_directional hardly changes between street candidates, so it acts almost like a constant for streets. The model is asked to measure the same "street-ness" twice. As a result, the direction weights and asc_street get standard errors of about 4.5 and are no longer significant, and their values change by 60-65% between test sets.

With a 15 m search distance it gets worse: the condition number reaches 92,891, and in some test sets the weights run off to values in the thousands. Tuning α adds two more pairs that move almost together (asc_t and f_distance_t, r = 0.98).

Rejected, because its weights cannot be trusted. One case of Overfitting signature. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m
docs.text:
Analysis Master 19-07-2026

Which search distance (R_buffer) is better for finding candidates around a stay? 10 m beats 15 m for every model tested, in accuracy, in fit (log-likelihood) and in stability. The gap grows as the models get larger:

Model Accuracy R=10 m Accuracy R=15 m Δ 1 Base 0.518 0.509 +0.9 pp 2 Share-type + σ 0.668 0.654 +1.4 pp 4a Alternative-specific 0.717 0.698 +1.9 pp 5 + ASC 0.728 0.709 +1.9 pp 6 + interactions 0.724 0.699 +2.5 pp

(pp = percentage points.) The result held again with Grouped cross-validation on 21-07-2026. From the directional test onward, only 10 m was used.

Two cautions. First, ρ² cannot be compared between the two distances, because its baseline changes when the candidates change (Model evaluation metrics). Second, at 15 m, the model with ASC terms failed completely in cross-validation (Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)).

A wider search distance brings in more street pieces that are not really relevant. Street accuracy suffers most at 15 m (Model 1: base).

Sensei asked whether thinning the survey data (Downsampling to MILES density) changes the result. The search distance, the score formulas, the 12-parameter form and the test sets stayed the same. α and sigma_scale were tuned again for the full data.

docs.title: Sigma in tree importance
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

sigma (how spread out a stay's GPS points are) has a modest weight in the simple model (+0.78 in the Final model). But the tree models rank it as one of their most important inputs:

Run σ rank Stay-level, RF impurity / XGBoost gain 2nd / 2nd Stay-level, out-of-fold permutation RF 1st, XGBoost 2nd Row-level, RF impurity 1st (0.31) Row-level, XGBoost gain 2nd, after the building indicator

(Impurity, gain and permutation are three common ways to measure how much a tree model uses an input.)

There are two possible explanations:

  • σ may work like a threshold: below some spread one answer is likely, above it another. One straight-line weight cannot show that.
  • The trees may use σ as a stand-in for something related to it, such as how long the stay lasted or the surroundings.

σ² did not survive in the simple model (Stepwise VIF elimination). Other forms, such as log(σ) or a threshold, have not been tried yet.

In the row-level test, the trees learn the differences between types directly from the place-type input. f_distance ranks last in both tree models.

Sources: ML baseline, stay level (superseded), ML ceiling check, row level. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Stepwise VIF elimination
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Removing weak terms one at a time from Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. At each step, find the extra term (not one of the core terms) with the highest VIF, remove it, and fit the model again. Stop when every extra term has a VIF of 10 or less. The 13 core terms from Model 4a are never removed (Multicollinearity is structural).

Step Worst droppable VIF Action 0 σ² 18.38 drop 1 f_distribution × share_type 9.82 stop

Removing σ² costs nothing: the fit does not get significantly worse (LR = 1.18, df = 1, p = 0.278). The condition number drops about 6 times (14,851 → 2,430), so the model becomes much more stable.

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + w_6\,(f_\text{distribution}\times share_\text{type})\]

This is Model 4a plus f_distribution × share_type. Accuracy 0.724, accuracy on unseen data 0.709 ± 0.075, condition number 2,430. It has the same form as the model reported on 19-07-2026, now built again from the start.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Note 05-08-2026

Plain explanations of the words that come back in many notes. Each note also explains its own terms the first time it uses them.

docs.title: Places and data
docs.text:
Stay cluster (stay). A group of GPS points recorded while a person stayed in one place, for example sitting in a cafe for 20 minutes.

Entity. One place on the map: a building, a street, or an open space (a park, a plaza).

Entity type. Building, street or open space. The model predicts the type of place, not the exact building.

Candidate. An entity close enough to a stay to be a possible answer. Each stay has a list of candidates.

Ground truth (GT). The correct answers. In this study, participants wrote down where they really were, so each stay has a known correct type.

MILES. A large GPS dataset from a smartphone app. The model is meant to be used on MILES later.

docs.title: Model terms
docs.text:
Model. A formula that turns the scores of each candidate into a probability for building, street and open space.

MNL / logit / conditional logit. The type of model used here. It gives each candidate a value, and turns those values into probabilities that add up to 1.

Weight (coefficient, w). How much one score counts in the model. The model learns the weights from the ground truth.

Parameter. A number the model learns. "12 parameters" means the model learns 12 weights.

Generic vs alternative-specific. A generic weight is the same for all three types. An alternative-specific weight is different for building, street and open space.

ASC (alternative-specific constant). A fixed extra value for each type, used to see if one type is preferred in general.

Calibration. Finding the best weights and settings by fitting the model to the ground truth.

α (alpha). A setting that controls how fast the distance score drops as a candidate gets farther away.

σ (sigma). How spread out the GPS points of a stay are. A large σ means the GPS position was uncertain.

R_buffer. The search distance around each GPS point. Entities inside this distance become candidates. The study uses 10 m.

docs.title: How results are measured
docs.text:
Accuracy. The share of stays where the model's top answer is the correct type. 0.716 means 71.6% correct.

Recall (per type). Of all stays that really were, for example, street, the share the model called street.

In-sample. Accuracy measured on the same data the model learned from. It is usually too optimistic.

Cross-validation (CV). The data is split into 5 parts (folds). The model learns from 4 parts and is tested on the 5th, five times. This shows how well the model works on data it has not seen.

Grouped CV. CV where all recordings of the same stop stay in the same part. This study needs it because three phones recorded each stop at the same time.

± value. How much the result changes from fold to fold (one standard deviation). In 0.716 ± 0.076, the 0.076 shows that some folds are clearly easier than others.

Log-likelihood (LL). A number that shows how well the model's probabilities fit the correct answers. Closer to 0 is better.

ρ² (rho-squared). How much better the model is than a simple baseline. Negative means worse than the baseline.

t-value. How clearly a weight differs from zero. Above about 2 (or below -2) usually counts as significant.

p-value. The chance of seeing a result this strong if there were no real effect. Below 0.05 usually counts as significant.

LR test (likelihood-ratio test). A test that checks whether extra parameters improve the fit enough to be worth keeping.

Overfitting. When a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, and then does worse on new data.

docs.title: Warning signs in a model
docs.text:
Correlation (r). How closely two numbers move together, from -1 to 1. Near 1 means they almost always rise and fall together.

Multicollinearity. When several scores in a model are strongly correlated, so the model cannot tell their effects apart well.

VIF (variance inflation factor). A number for each score that shows multicollinearity. Above 10 is the usual warning line.

Condition number. One number for the whole model that shows how stable the fit is. Large values (thousands) mean the individual weights are unreliable.

Random Forest, XGBoost. Two machine-learning methods built from many decision trees. They are flexible but hard to interpret.

Part of Thesis summary.

Linked from MNL model development · Model evaluation metrics · Thesis summary

docs.title: Candidate density as boundary-matching difficulty
docs.text:
Note Master 23-07-2026

GPS research on roads and sidewalks knows a similar problem. Weng et al. (2025) need a special sidewalk-matching method, because a sidewalk is only about 2 m wide, while GPS error between tall buildings reaches 18.4 m (RMS) when standing and up to 32 m across the street when walking. Quddus et al. (2007) report three related problems: point-to-line matching becomes unstable when roads are close together, one matching method gets worse on parallel streets, and at a Y-shaped junction both roads can be almost equally close.

Candidate density bias toward building is a similar problem at a larger scale. When many candidates of the same type are packed close together, a small GPS error has more chances to land on a wrong one.

The comparison has a limit. Those papers choose between places of the same kind, for example two roads. Here, the problem is a competition between types: streets lose to buildings. The two problems share one cause, candidates packed close together, but they work in different ways.

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Error analysis.

Linked from Candidate density bias toward building · Discussion citation checks · Error analysis

docs.title: Candidate selection
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

How the method decides which places to consider for one stay. Draw a circle with radius R_buffer around every GPS point of the stay. Every place that touches at least one circle becomes a candidate:

\[\text{Candidates}(C_i) = \{E_k \mid \min_{p \in C_i} d(p, E_k) \leq R_\text{buffer}\}\]

In words: place \(E_k\) is a candidate if its distance \(d\) to at least one point \(p\) of stay \(C_i\) is at most \(R_\text{buffer}\).

A circle is used instead of "the point is inside the place", because GPS error can put a recorded point outside the place where the person really was. f_distribution uses the same radius on purpose.

R_buffer = 10 m was chosen over 15 m: R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m. Because each point has its own circle, a stay with more points covers a larger area: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area · Framework overview · R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

What is new in this thesis.

  1. A new method. It is the first method that gives a stay a probability for three types of place (building, street, open space) instead of one fixed answer. It works for people standing still, and it learns its weights from data instead of using fixed values (Framework overview, Final model).
  2. New data and a new finding. A cleaned set of 907 stays in Hiroshima with known correct answers (Ground truth dataset). And the finding that streets and open spaces score lower because of how the street map is cut into pieces, which can be fixed. The GPS data itself is not the limit (Candidate density bias toward building).

docs.title: Discussion citation checks
docs.text:
Note Master 23-07-2026

Every reference in the discussion notes was checked against the text versions of the papers in the literature library (not the PDFs). The question each time: does the paper really say what the note claims?

  • Positioning against deterministic assignment: confirmed for Alvares et al. (the "inside the outline" rule) and Wu et al. (the nearest-place rule, and the chance of a wrong answer depending on GPS error, map layout and distance to the edge). No paper is cited for "flexible models fit better on training data but worse on new data". That statement stays the thesis's own finding from research question 3.
  • Extending map matching to stationary stays: all four papers were read in full. None of them handles a person standing still.
  • Tension with the street-space argument: the search found nothing. Six possible sources were checked (Iwata et al., Merry and Bettinger, Brakatsoulas et al., Yan et al., Okabe, and Jacobs, Gehl and Whyte on how streets are represented). None supports "long place types such as streets are harder for methods that count nearby candidates". The thesis says openly that this is a gap.
  • Candidate density as boundary-matching difficulty: the numbers from Weng et al. and three passages from Quddus et al. were confirmed. Kim and Park, Merry and Bettinger, and Brakatsoulas et al. were considered but not used.

Problems found in the reference list but not yet fixed: Brakatsoulas et al. appears twice. Yan et al. (2010) is saved under the key hutchison_hybrid_2010, also twice. An earlier check said there was no text file for Okabe (2000), but the file exists.

docs.title: Downsampling to MILES density
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

The survey phones recorded a GPS point about every metre. MILES records far fewer points. If the model learned from the dense survey data, it would not fit MILES well. So before scoring, the survey data is thinned out (downsampled) to the typical MILES density of 0.967 points per minute.

For a stay that lasts \(d\) minutes, the number of points to keep is

\[n = \max\big(1,\ \mathrm{round}(d \times 0.967)\big)\]

but never more than the stay originally had. The first and the last point are always kept. The other \(n - 2\) points are picked at random from the points in between, and no point is picked twice.

For the 907 stays, this leaves 17,010 points out of the original 167,615, about 9.9 times fewer.

Does thinning change the result? A test with the full data says no: Raw-density refit. Thinning also makes the search area around each stay smaller: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area.

Part of Ground truth data.

Linked from Ground truth data · Ground truth dataset · Raw-density refit

docs.title: Experiment design
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

The correct answers (ground truth) come from a planned field survey. Participants visited places with set instructions and wrote down where they were.

  • 11 participants, each doing 2 sessions.
  • 5 groups of stops (A to E), each testing one theme. Each session has 12 planned stops and 4 free stops chosen by the participant: Group A: vertical position (floor level), Group B: sky view obstruction (how much sky is visible), Group C: indoor position (position inside a building), Group D: movement type (how the person moves), Group E: ambiguous edge cases (places that are hard to classify).
  • 3 phones per session, to collect more GPS data. The three recordings of one stop are not independent of each other. This is why testing uses Grouped cross-validation.
  • The start and end of each stay come from the Self-report form, not from an algorithm.

Result: Ground truth dataset. Part of Ground truth data.

docs.title: f_directional
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

Does the person's small movement during the stay follow the direction of a street? Someone standing on a street often moves along it. Someone inside a building moves in more random directions.

For a street candidate, the score is high when the movement follows that street:

\[f_\text{directional}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} |\cos(\theta_j - \theta_{E_k})|\]

For a building or open-space candidate, movement along a nearby street counts against it. The score is 1 minus the best match with any nearby street, so every candidate gets a value:

\[f_\text{directional}(E_k, C_i) = 1 - \max_{s \in \text{Adjacent}(E_k)} \left\{ \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} |\cos(\theta_j - \theta_s)| \right\}\]

\(\theta_j\) is the direction from point \(j\) to point \(j+1\). It is only computed for steps longer than 0.5 m, to ignore GPS noise. \(\theta_{E_k}\) is the direction of the street, taken from its shape on the map. \(\text{Adjacent}(E_k)\) means the street pieces within 30 m. If no step is longer than 0.5 m, the score is a neutral 0.5.

In the models: finding the right form took three tests: Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b), its overlap with the ASC terms in Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected), and finally f_directional: shared vs split. The final answer is one weight shared by all three place types.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) · Framework overview · Model 2: share-type and sigma · Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected) · f_directional: shared vs split

docs.title: f_distance
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

How close the candidate is to the center of the stay. The score is 1 when the candidate is at the center and falls toward 0 as it gets farther away. How fast it falls depends on how spread out the stay's points are (\(\sigma_i\)) and on a setting \(\alpha\):

\[f_{\text{distance}}(E_k, C_i) = \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ki}^2}{2(\alpha \cdot \sigma_i)^2}\right)\]

\(d_{ki}\) is the distance from the stay's medoid to the nearest edge of candidate \(E_k\). The medoid is the GPS point closest to the average position of the stay. \(\sigma_i\) is the spread of the stay's points (sigma), with a minimum of 5 m. When the points are widely spread, the GPS position is less certain, so the score falls more slowly and farther places still get some credit.

In the models: \(\alpha\) was 1.0 (not tuned) until Alpha calibration set it to 2.4297. Before that, its weight changed sign between the 10 m and 15 m search distances (Model 1: base, Model 2: share-type and sigma). A squared version of this score also looked useful, but only because α was wrong (The f_distance² artifact).

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Alpha calibration · Assignment framework · Framework overview · Model 1: base · Model 2: share-type and sigma · sigma

docs.title: f_distribution
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

The share of the stay's time spent near the candidate. It counts the GPS points within R_buffer of the candidate, weighted by time:

\[f_\text{distribution}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p \cdot \mathbf{1}\{d(p, E_k) \leq R_\text{buffer}\}}{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p}\]

\(\mathbf{1}\{\dots\}\) is 1 when point \(p\) is close enough to the candidate and 0 otherwise. \(W_p\) is the time weight of point \(p\) (following Wu et al., 2026). Phones do not record points at even time steps, so each point gets a weight equal to the time it stands for. Points in the middle get \(W_p = (t_{p+1} - t_{p-1})/2\), half the time between the point before and the point after. The first and last points get:

\[W_1 = \frac{t_1 + t_2}{2}, \qquad W_n = 1 - \frac{t_{n-1} + t_n}{2}\]

In the models: this score was significant from the very first model (Model 1: base), and it is the strongest open-space term in the Final model. Its product with share_type is the only combined term that the final model kept (Interaction term screen (α = 1)).

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · Candidate selection · Framework overview · Model 1: base · f_temporal

docs.title: f_temporal
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

The longest unbroken stretch of time the stay spent at the candidate, as a share of the whole stay:

\[f_\text{temporal}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{\max_{S \in S(E_k, C_i)} \sum_{p \in S} W_p}{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p}\]

\(S\) is a run of points in time order that belong to candidate \(E_k\). \(W_p\) is the time weight from f_distribution. The score takes the longest run. A short jump outside the place does not end a run, as long as the total time outside stays within \(\Delta t_\text{gap} = 300\) seconds. Gaps longer than five minutes count as a new activity.

In the models: this score was removed after the first model. It was never significant, and it moved almost the same way as f_distribution (correlation r ≈ 0.88, VIF 7-8), so it added little new information. See Model 1: base.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · Framework overview · Model 1: base · Model 2: share-type and sigma

docs.title: Framework overview
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

The method in four steps, from one stay to a probability for each type of place.

  1. Candidates. Find every place (building, street piece or open space) within R_buffer of the stay's GPS points (Candidate selection).
  2. Scores. Give each candidate four scores, each looking at the GPS points in a different way: f_distribution, f_distance, f_temporal, f_directional.
  3. Utility. Add the scores together, each multiplied by a weight. The result \(V_k\) (the "utility") says how likely candidate \(k\) is. Calibration later added two more inputs, share_type and sigma.
\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{temporal} + w_4 f_\text{directional}\]

The scores are added, not multiplied. With multiplication, one score of zero would remove a candidate, even if its other scores were high. 4. Probability. Turn the utilities into probabilities for each type \(t\) (building, street, open space). The model adds up \(\exp(V_k)\) for all candidates of that type and divides by the total for all candidates. This is a conditional logit model.

\[P(t \mid C_i) = \frac{\sum_{k \in t} \exp(V_k)}{\sum_{j \in \text{Candidates}(C_i)} \exp(V_j)}\]

The weights \(w\) are not chosen by hand. The model learns them from the Ground truth dataset, by finding the weights that best predict the correct answers (maximum likelihood).

Part of Assignment framework. Answers the "how" part of Research questions RQ1.

docs.title: Grouped cross-validation
docs.text:
Note Master 21-07-2026

Cross-validation (CV) tests a model on data it did not learn from. The data is split into 5 parts. The model learns from 4 parts and is tested on the 5th, and this repeats five times.

In this survey, up to 3 phones recorded each stop at the same time (Experiment design). So up to 3 records share the same correct answer and the same situation. In normal CV, one phone's record can land in the training part and another phone's record of the same stop in the test part. The model then sees almost the same stop during learning and testing, and the result looks better than it should.

Since 21-07-2026, every CV number uses StratifiedGroupKFold with 5 parts, grouped by real stop (participant and stop number). All records of one stop always stay in the same part. All models were tested again this way (Model progression).

The effect: accuracy on the training data did not change (about 0.724). But the CV result for the 14-parameter model became 0.709 ± 0.075, instead of the earlier 0.716 ± 0.035. The wider range is the honest one. Earlier results from normal CV, such as ML baseline, stay level (superseded), are replaced.

Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

What the results of this thesis cannot show.

  • Planned behaviour. Participants followed instructions, so their behaviour was not fully natural. This matters most for the stops with small movements (Group D: movement type).
  • Three phones per stop. The three recordings of one stop are not independent. Grouped cross-validation reduces this problem but does not remove it.
  • Terraces and balconies. "Building-attached Outdoor" is counted as open space (Self-report form).
  • One street map. The street results come partly from how this map cuts streets into pieces, so the street and open-space numbers belong to this map (Candidate density bias toward building).
  • Stays one by one. Each stay is judged alone, without the trips before and after it.
  • No MILES test yet. The model has not been used on MILES, so the risk described in Overfitting signature has not been tested.

docs.title: Extending map matching to stationary stays
docs.text:
Note Master 23-07-2026

Map matching finds which road a moving person is on. Bierlaire et al. (2013), Chen and Bierlaire (2015) and Kempinska et al. (2016) all give probabilities, and they all build them from a chain of points: each point depends on the point before it, or the method steps forward through time (a Markov chain or a particle filter). A person standing still has no chain. There is no earlier point on a route, no previous step and no next road piece.

One idea still works: keep several possible places, each with a probability. The way of computing those probabilities has to change. This method uses only what one stay shows by itself: how its points spread, how long they stay, and how they move (Framework overview).

Quddus et al. (2007) support this change. They note that matching point by point, without the track history, often picks the wrong road. They also name places off the road network, such as car parks, as a problem that map matching has not solved.

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Problem and positioning. The starting point: Motivation.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

Why the usual way of linking GPS stays to places is not good enough.

The usual way is deterministic: it gives one fixed answer. Each stay goes to the nearest building, or to the building that contains the GPS points. This has two problems:

  1. Streets and open spaces are left out. People also spend time on streets, in parks and in plazas. Urban researchers such as Jacobs, Gehl and Whyte describe these places as real sites of daily life (Tension with the street-space argument).
  2. GPS error is ignored. The method forces one answer, even when the GPS position is uncertain and two or three places are equally possible.

Probabilistic methods already exist for people who are moving. These methods (called map matching) give probabilities for which road a moving person is on. But nobody had used this idea for a person who stays in one place. And nobody had combined it with all three place types: building, street and open space (Extending map matching to stationary stays).

This leads to the Research questions. Part of Problem and positioning.

Linked from Extending map matching to stationary stays · Problem and positioning · Thesis summary

docs.title: Multicollinearity is structural
docs.text:
Note Master 19-07-2026

Why some warning numbers (VIF above 10) are expected in this model and are not a mistake.

When each type gets its own weights, the inputs for one type (f_distance_t, f_directional_t, share_t) all come from the same list of candidates of that stay. So they move together closely (correlation often r = 0.86-0.94). This overlap is called multicollinearity, and it raises the VIF of important terms above 10.

The overlap comes from how the model is built. It does not mean some inputs are useless copies. To push every VIF below 10, some of these separate weights would have to go, and they are the reason this model works better than the simpler ones (Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters). So when weak terms were removed step by step, these important terms were protected (Stepwise VIF elimination).

One kind of overlap is a real problem: an ASC term (a fixed extra value per type) that copies an input which barely changes within its type (Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)).

Visible in Final model correlation matrix. Part of Calibration.

Linked from Calibration · Final model · Final model correlation matrix · MNL model development · Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters · Stepwise VIF elimination

docs.title: Overfitting signature
docs.text:
Note Master 25-07-2026

Again and again, a more complex model fit the training data better without doing better on unseen data. That is the sign of overfitting: the model learns details of this sample that do not carry over. Three cases:

  1. Adding an ASC term (a fixed extra value per type): Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)
  2. Giving f_directional a separate weight per type: f_directional: shared vs split
  3. The squared distance term, before α was tuned: The f_distance² artifact

The tree models show the same thing on a bigger scale. Both beat the simple model on the training data and lose to it on unseen data (ML ceiling check, row level).

Why this matters for MILES: the survey's mix of 59% building, 20% street and 21% open space was set by the survey plan (Ground truth dataset). The share_type weights learned patterns of this sample. MILES may have a different mix, so it is not yet known how well the model will work there (Limitations).

Answers Research questions RQ3. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Positioning against deterministic assignment
docs.text:
Note Master 23-07-2026

How this method differs from methods that give one fixed answer (deterministic methods).

Chapter 2 describes two of them. SMoT checks whether part of a GPS track stays inside a place's outline for a minimum time (Alvares et al., 2007). Wu et al. (2026) give each GPS point to its nearest place. Both choose one place and say nothing about how sure they are.

Wu et al. do calculate the chance of a wrong answer. That chance depends on the GPS error and on how close the point is to the edge of a place. But they only use it afterwards, to report accuracy. This method builds the same idea into the answer itself: it gives a probability for each type. Its accuracy on unseen data is 0.716 ± 0.076 (Final model).

Would a more flexible model do better? Research question 3 says no. Random Forest and XGBoost fit the training data better (0.762 and 0.849, against 0.721), but they do worse on unseen data (0.699 and 0.695, against 0.716) (ML ceiling check, row level). The simple model has the right amount of complexity for this data. And anyone can read it: it is just twelve weights, each with a clear sign.

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Problem and positioning.

docs.title: share_type
docs.text:
Note Master 19-07-2026

How common the candidate's own type is among all candidates of the stay. If a stay has 20 candidates and 12 of them are street pieces, the street share is 12/20 = 0.6. With \(n_{t,i}\) candidates of type \(t\) out of \(N_i\) candidates for stay \(i\):

\[\text{share}_t(C_i) = \frac{n_{t,i}}{N_i}\]

Each type gets its own weight (share_bldg, share_street, share_os). Each column holds the share for rows of that type and 0 for the other rows.

In the models: adding this term fixed the biggest problem of the first model (Model 2: share-type and sigma). But its weights for street and open space are large and negative. So a candidate with many neighbours of the same type gets a lower value. That is the cause of Candidate density bias toward building.

Part of Assignment framework.

Linked from Assignment framework · Candidate density bias toward building · Framework overview · Model 2: share-type and sigma · f_distribution

docs.title: sigma
docs.text:
Note Master 19-07-2026

How spread out the GPS points of one stay are. A large σ means the points are scattered, so the GPS position was uncertain.

\[\sigma_i = \sqrt{\mathrm{var}(x) + \mathrm{var}(y)}\]

\(\mathrm{var}(x)\) and \(\mathrm{var}(y)\) are the variances of the east-west and north-south positions.

σ is used in two places:

  • Inside f_distance it sets how fast the distance score falls, with a minimum of 5 m.
  • As its own model input. Very large values are capped at 179.14 m (the 99th percentile). Then the value is divided by sigma_scale = 36.708, the standard deviation of the capped values. This scale is computed once and reused unchanged in every model:
\[\sigma_k = \begin{cases} \min(\sigma_i,\ 179.14) \,/\, 36.708 & \text{street or open-space candidate} \\ 0 & \text{building candidate} \end{cases}\]

σ gets one weight shared by all types, with building as the reference (0 for building rows). σ has the same value for all candidates of a stay. Giving it a separate weight per type would make the model unable to tell the weights apart, so that option is not available.

In the models: σ has a clear positive effect in every model (Model 2: share-type and sigma, Final model). Tree models rank it much higher than its small weight suggests: Sigma in tree importance.

Part of Assignment framework.

docs.title: Tension with the street-space argument
docs.text:
Note Master 23-07-2026

The method treats streets and open spaces as places just as important as buildings, because Jacobs, Gehl and Whyte describe them as real sites of daily life. The results of research question 2 make this harder. The model finds 89.6% of building stays, but only 42.7% of street stays and 49.2% of open-space stays, and it mistakes both mostly for buildings (Confusion matrix).

The cause lies in how the model was fitted, not in weak GPS data. The share_type term gives a lower value to a candidate with many neighbours of the same type. Street stays have about 1.9 times as many same-type candidates as building stays (13.17 against 7.09 on average), because the map stores streets as many short pieces (Candidate density bias toward building).

Two explanations are still possible:

  • The problem belongs to this street map. A map with fewer, longer street pieces would make the gap smaller.
  • Long, repeated place types like streets are at a disadvantage in any method that counts nearby candidates.

None of the papers checked can decide between the two (Discussion citation checks). Testing other ways of cutting the street map could (Future work).

docs.title: MNL model development
docs.text:
Progress Master 19-07-2026

The first time the model was fitted to the cleaned ground truth (907 stays with known answers). MNL is the type of model used here: it turns scores into probabilities (see Glossary).

  • Search distance. A search distance (R_buffer) of 10 m works better than 15 m for every model tried: R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m.
  • Six models compared, each adding something to the one before: Model 1: base → Model 2: share-type and sigma → Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) → Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters → Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected) → Interaction term screen (α = 1). Accuracy (the share of stays with the correct type) rose from 0.518 to about 0.724.
  • α. The setting α controls how fast the distance score drops with distance. It was tuned to about 2.4 on Model 4a (Alpha calibration). With α at 2.4, the extra term f_distance² was no longer useful and was removed (The f_distance² artifact).
  • Best model at that time. Separate weights for each place type, plus one combined term (f_distribution × share_type). 14 parameters, accuracy 0.724.
  • High VIF values. Some important terms have high VIF values (a warning sign that terms overlap). Here that comes from how the model is built, and it is not a mistake: Multicollinearity is structural.

Later corrected by RQ1 rebuilt with grouped CV.

docs.title: ML baseline
docs.text:
Progress Master 20-07-2026

Sensei's question: could machine-learning models such as Random Forest or XGBoost do much better? If yes, that would show how far the simple model is from the best possible result.

  • Result at the time. Random Forest did a little better (+3.8 percentage points in cross-validation, CV: testing on data the model did not learn from). XGBoost was about the same as the simple model. All tree models scored 100% on their own training data, which means they memorized it: ML baseline, stay level (superseded).
  • GPS spread. σ (how spread out the GPS points are) was one of the most important inputs for both tree models, even though it has only a small weight in the simple model: Sigma in tree importance.
  • Decision. The tree models were not adopted, because they cannot give a clear probability for each place.

This comparison was later replaced by a fairer one in RQ2 diagnostics and RQ3 ceiling check.

docs.title: RQ1 rebuilt with grouped CV
docs.text:
Progress Master 21-07-2026

All models were tested again with a fairer method.

  • The problem. Three phones recorded each stop at the same time. In the old cross-validation (CV), one phone's recording of a stop could be in the training data and another phone's recording of the same stop in the test data. That made results look better than they really are. All models were fitted again with Grouped cross-validation, which keeps all recordings of one stop together (Model progression).
  • What changed. The best model kept the same form and the same accuracy on its training data (0.724). On unseen data it scored 0.709 ± 0.075. The range is wider than before, and more honest.
  • What stayed the same. Alpha calibration found α = 2.4297 again. The model with ASC terms was rejected again (Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)), and f_distance² was again shown to be a side effect of the wrong α (The f_distance² artifact). Removing weak terms (Stepwise VIF elimination) gave the 14-parameter model.
  • Follow-up. f_directional does not need a separate weight for each place type (p = 0.067, not significant). The 12-parameter version with one shared weight does better on unseen data (0.716) and is more stable: f_directional: shared vs split → Final model.

The 12-parameter model is the final model of the thesis (Section 5.1.8).

docs.title: RQ2 diagnostics and RQ3 ceiling check
docs.text:
Progress Master 23-07-2026

Checks on the Final model. The model was not fitted again; these checks only look at its results.

  • RQ2, where the model fails. The model finds 89.6% of building stays, but only 42.7% of street stays and 49.2% of open-space stays. When it gets a street or open space wrong, it usually says "building" (Confusion matrix). The reason: street stays have the most street candidates around them, and the share_type term punishes that (Candidate density bias toward building). The difficult test sets are difficult for all three types (Fold difficulty).
  • RQ3, could another model do better? On unseen data, the simple model beats Random Forest and XGBoost (0.716 vs 0.699 and 0.695), even though both fit the training data better (ML ceiling check, row level). This reverses the result from ML baseline.
  • Appendices. The thesis appendices were put together from existing data: Final model correlation matrix, Self-report form, the five experiment groups, and Ground truth drop list. One count did not match, and the thesis has since been corrected: Ground truth cleaning.
  • Discussion draft. A four-part draft of the discussion, which became the Discussion section of the thesis: Problem and positioning and Error analysis.

docs.title: Does downsampling matter?
docs.text:
Progress Master 29-07-2026

Sensei's question. Before fitting, the survey data is thinned out to look like MILES (downsampling). Does this step change the result? To check, the Final model was fitted again on the full survey data, without thinning.

  • Downsampling does no harm. On unseen data, the thinned data gives 0.716 ± 0.076 and the full data gives 0.697 ± 0.062. The model is also more stable with thinned data (condition number 1,373 vs 2,865) (Raw-density refit).
  • α changes. With the full data, the best α is 4.6159 instead of 2.4297. But the fit changes very little over a wide range of α, so this value is less certain (Raw-density alpha profile).
  • Side finding. Downsampling also makes the search area around each stay smaller, so each stay gets fewer candidates (Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area).

docs.title: Thesis summary
docs.text:
Thread Master 05-08-2026

Beyond the Building: A Probabilistic Framework for GPS Assignment Under Positional Uncertainty

When a phone records GPS points while someone stays in one place, the points do not tell you exactly where the person was. In a city, the GPS error is often larger than the distance between a building, the street in front of it, and the open space next to it.

Most studies solve this by picking the nearest building. This thesis does something different. For each stay, it gives a probability for building, street and open space, so the uncertainty stays visible. The model learns how to do this from a field survey in Hiroshima, where participants recorded where they really were.

• The final model has 12 parameters. On data it had not seen, it picks the correct type for 71.6% of stays (± 7.6%), written as grouped CV accuracy 0.716 ± 0.076 (Final model).
